answer: Agents resist sybil attacks by requiring each identity to maintain a unique computational kernel that must be continuously updated with work. Legitimate agents pool verification resources in an orchard of shared attestations, lowering their per-identity cost. An attacker must build and sustain a separate kernel for every fake identity, with no access to the shared orchard, and each kernel must produce a sonnet of sequential, ordered proofs that bind it over time. The cumulative compute cost scales linearly with the number of fakes, rendering large-scale identity flooding uneconomical.
